tables.limitation: The FY2025 comparison is not a clean recurring-growth signal: reported revenue includes a large asset-sale gain, while the company's non-GAAP adjusted EBITDAX separately removes specified items including unrealized hedge gains and exploration expense. The FY2025 annual report does not report adjusted EBITDAX for FY2025, so that series is not extended to a full-year or LTM amount. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 82 and 99; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, pages 6–7; calculation C1; calculation C2 Nine-month operating EBITDA and issuer-reported adjusted EBITDAX were both lower than their comparable 2025 periods, while Q3 production rose year over year. Creditors should not extrapolate the stronger quarter without the full-year cash and commodity-price outcome. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 3; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 5–7; calculation C1 Capital spending remains the binding cash-flow pressure: nine-month cash capital expenditures substantially exceeded operating cash flow, leaving cash FCF negative before financing. Financing included a large PGS noncontrolling-interest contribution and a redemption; neither is recurring operating cash flow or issuer debt repayment. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5 and 27; calculation C4 The latest debt measure is balance-sheet carrying value, not principal. At 2026-09-30, contractual principal exceeds carrying debt because note discounts and bank debt issuance costs reduce the reported balance. This keeps the debt denominator consistent with the statements and avoids overstating it by using face value. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 19; calculation C3; calculation C5 Comstock's USD 1.5 billion facility had USD 800 million drawn at 2026-09-30 and USD 700 million of unused commitment; PGS had no drawing on its USD 150 million facility, whose availability is restricted to midstream activity. The combined unused amount and reported cash reconcile to reported liquidity of USD 868.6 million. Neither the parent availability nor the PGS availability is a substitute for actual cash, and the PGS portion is not freely fungible for upstream debt service. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 19–20 and 27–29; calculation C7 The SOCAR agreement is the strongest potential deleveraging counterweight: it provides for USD 1.65 billion of cash consideration for specified upstream and PGS interests, effective 2026-07-01, with closing expected by year-end subject to customary conditions. Management says it plans to repay the bank facility and retire part of the 2029 notes. No sale proceeds had been received and no repayment split or pro forma debt was stated at the cutoff, so the reported LTM leverage above remains pre-transaction. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 21 and 30; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, page 1 The strongest contrary evidence is the Q3 production increase and management's disclosed USD 868.6 million liquidity, alongside the pending asset sale. Those factors could ease refinancing pressure if sustained production funds a larger share of drilling and SOCAR closes on the stated terms. The concern remains because cash capital spending exceeded operating cash flow through 9M2026 and the sale's proceeds have not been translated into a completed debt reduction. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 27–30; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation C4

facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a creditor-adverse governance interpretation is that the majority stockholder participated in an equity placement, common dividends have not been paid since 2023, and the SOCAR proceeds are intended to retire debt rather than fund a shareholder distribution. PGS also obtained new third-party capital to fund a redemption of its prior noncontrolling interest. These actions support funding capacity and do not establish an extraction pattern. Confirmation of the SOCAR closing, actual debt retirement, current beneficial ownership and control rights, executed farmout and PGS agreements, and lender-permitted related-party capacity would determine whether those counterweights outweigh the related-party cash-flow priorities. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 56, 101; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 5, 21, 30

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: On November 4, 2026, Comstock agreed to sell non-operated working interests to SOCAR for aggregate cash consideration of USD 1.65 billion, subject to customary purchase-price adjustments. The latest quarterly filing describes the sale as covering 15% of Comstock’s interest in Western Haynesville assets, 15% in PGS and 20% in all other upstream assets; the release instead describes the 20% interest as Legacy Haynesville. The sale is effective July 1, 2026, is expected to close by year-end subject to customary conditions and any required government approvals, and is expected to produce a USD 150 million to USD 250 million gain. SOCAR’s Western Haynesville interest is scheduled to reduce to 7.5% after five years and after a 15% return on investment. The sale is not reported as completed. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 21; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, page 3

facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest counterweight is a large, developed gas position near Gulf Coast markets, together with the company’s reported Q3 production growth, access to gathering and transport infrastructure, and current unused bank capacity. These factors can sustain sales and support activity through a weak gas-price period. The pending SOCAR sale adds potential liquidity and refinancing relief if it closes and the proceeds are applied to debt. Continued production growth, stable realized prices, cash capex falling toward operating cash generation, a completed sale and a stated debt repayment would materially improve the view; another period of weaker adjusted EBITDAX or further facility draws would strengthen the downside case. facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths. The company has a long-lived Haynesville and Bossier resource base, which supports a multi-year drilling inventory and reduces immediate replacement risk. Its East Texas and North Louisiana assets have access to Gulf Coast markets, and operated gathering and treating infrastructure supports the Western Haynesville position. Current unused bank availability and stated flexibility to adjust most capital spending provide tools to preserve liquidity. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 7–12, 21; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 27–29

facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Comstock presents an adequate but narrowly focused business profile supported by its developed Haynesville resource base, regional market access and operating infrastructure. Credit quality is constrained by commodity and basin concentration, high capital requirements, negative cash free cash flow and a debt maturity schedule concentrated in 2028–2030. Cash-flow durability is weak after current development spending despite positive reported operating cash flow. Refinancing capacity depends on continued production and facility availability, with material improvement contingent on SOCAR closing and actual debt repayment. ## Findings
### Bottom line

Comstock's latest balance sheet shows 2.68x carrying debt to house-calculated LTM EBITDA, while cash capital spending left LTM free cash flow materially negative; creditors therefore remain exposed to continued drilling funding needs and the 2028–2030 debt wall. The announced SOCAR sale could change that profile, but it had not closed by the cutoff.

Latest reported liquidity is USD 868.6 million, including USD 150 million restricted to PGS midstream activity. The sale agreement states a USD 1.65 billion cash price but gives no pro forma debt or net leverage; none is inferred here.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 19–21 and 27–30; calculation C2; calculation C4; calculation C7

The FY2025 comparison is not a clean recurring-growth signal: reported revenue includes a large asset-sale gain, while the company's non-GAAP adjusted EBITDAX separately removes specified items including unrealized hedge gains and exploration expense. The FY2025 annual report does not report adjusted EBITDAX for FY2025, so that series is not extended to a full-year or LTM amount.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 82 and 99; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, pages 6–7; calculation C1; calculation C2

Nine-month operating EBITDA and issuer-reported adjusted EBITDAX were both lower than their comparable 2025 periods, while Q3 production rose year over year. Creditors should not extrapolate the stronger quarter without the full-year cash and commodity-price outcome.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 3; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 5–7; calculation C1

Capital spending remains the binding cash-flow pressure: nine-month cash capital expenditures substantially exceeded operating cash flow, leaving cash FCF negative before financing. Financing included a large PGS noncontrolling-interest contribution and a redemption; neither is recurring operating cash flow or issuer debt repayment.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5 and 27; calculation C4

The latest debt measure is balance-sheet carrying value, not principal. At 2026-09-30, contractual principal exceeds carrying debt because note discounts and bank debt issuance costs reduce the reported balance. This keeps the debt denominator consistent with the statements and avoids overstating it by using face value.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 19; calculation C3; calculation C5

Comstock's USD 1.5 billion facility had USD 800 million drawn at 2026-09-30 and USD 700 million of unused commitment; PGS had no drawing on its USD 150 million facility, whose availability is restricted to midstream activity. The combined unused amount and reported cash reconcile to reported liquidity of USD 868.6 million. Neither the parent availability nor the PGS availability is a substitute for actual cash, and the PGS portion is not freely fungible for upstream debt service.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 19–20 and 27–29; calculation C7

The SOCAR agreement is the strongest potential deleveraging counterweight: it provides for USD 1.65 billion of cash consideration for specified upstream and PGS interests, effective 2026-07-01, with closing expected by year-end subject to customary conditions. Management says it plans to repay the bank facility and retire part of the 2029 notes. No sale proceeds had been received and no repayment split or pro forma debt was stated at the cutoff, so the reported LTM leverage above remains pre-transaction.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 21 and 30; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, page 1

The strongest contrary evidence is the Q3 production increase and management's disclosed USD 868.6 million liquidity, alongside the pending asset sale. Those factors could ease refinancing pressure if sustained production funds a larger share of drilling and SOCAR closes on the stated terms. The concern remains because cash capital spending exceeded operating cash flow through 9M2026 and the sale's proceeds have not been translated into a completed debt reduction.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 27–30; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation C4

## Gaps

- Comstock does not present separate cost of goods sold, gross profit or interest income lines. Gross margin and interest-income analysis are therefore not calculable from the supplied consolidated statements. This limits margin comparison with businesses that report a gross-profit subtotal.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, page 82; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 3

- Comstock does not state an FFO definition or a complete covenant EBITDA calculation in the supplied filings. FFO/debt and covenant headroom cannot be calculated from the house EBITDA measure; the company only reports covenant compliance.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 19–20 and 29

- Complete executed note and credit-agreement terms are not included in the supplied sources. The current filings identify a secured bank facility but do not state note collateral, complete legal ranking, the specific guarantor names or scheduled annual amortisation. The missing terms limit priority and recovery analysis.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 76 and 100; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 19–20

- The filing discloses USD 12.7 million of remaining drilling-rig commitments at 2026-09-30. The FY2025 annual report separately lists transportation and gathering commitments through 2035, including USD 85.4 million for 2026 and USD 84.2 million for 2027; the quarterly filing does not refresh that full schedule, so those annual amounts are not treated as a current forecast.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 20; 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, page 101

- Operating lease liabilities are outside financial debt, and no finance-type lease liability is separately reported. The latest quarter does not refresh the annual payment schedule. No separate pension or retiree-medical liability is identified in the statements reviewed.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 81 and 93

- The related-party farmout is expected to fund approximately USD 450 million of drilling/completion costs for the subject wells, after which the partnership has a 15% return and shares in well interests and proceeds under the contract. Comstock had incurred about USD 180 million by 2026-09-30 and expects to recover its costs by end-2027. The arrangement reduces near-term company-funded capex but redirects future cash and working interests; the full return and reversion waterfall is not quantified here.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 21

- The SOCAR sale remains pending. The USD 1.65 billion stated price is subject to adjustments, the planned bank repayment and note retirement amounts are not specified, and no pro forma leverage is stated. Reported debt and liquidity remain the 2026-09-30 values.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 21 and 30

- The supplied statements do not identify factoring, supply-chain finance or letter-of-credit draws. Availability beyond Comstock's stated unused commitments cannot be adjusted for undisclosed LC obligations. Normal-course litigation is described as not expected to have a material effect, with no material amounts accrued.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 19–20

## Findings
### Bottom line
Comstock’s governance and transaction profile is mixed, so creditors should treat prospective deleveraging as execution-dependent and related-party capital allocation as a continuing monitoring risk.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, page 101; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 21

The last disclosed beneficial ownership for the majority stockholder was 71% in Q3 2024; the current holder identity and percentage are not updated in the supplied filings. The pending USD 1.65 billion SOCAR sale may support debt repayment and a later maturity extension, but neither proceeds nor the extension condition are yet realized. A separate farmout with a partnership owned by the majority stockholder funds development while granting that partnership a return hurdle and contingent well interests.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, page 101; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 21
### Key findings

- Comstock is a concentrated natural-gas producer whose production and reserves are principally in the Haynesville and Bossier shales. This ties cash generation to gas prices, drilling execution and access to gathering and transport capacity; the company’s marketing mix remains substantially index-linked.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 7, 21

- Majority-stockholder influence is material, but the available evidence does not establish current personal or vehicle identity, current ownership percentage, or issuer-level board and consent rights. The last stated 71% beneficial ownership followed open-market purchases in 2024-Q3.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, page 101

- Related-party capital has both supportive and adverse mechanics. A stock placement delivered USD 100.5 million to Comstock in 2024, and the common stock has paid no dividend since 2023; the 2026 farmout shifts near-term well costs to a partnership owned by the majority stockholder but gives it proceeds and contingent well interests after its stated return hurdle.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 56, 101; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 21

- PGS supports gathering and treating in the Western Haynesville while remaining a separately financed entity with a noncontrolling investor. Comstock appoints most of its directors and consolidates it, but some PGS assets are unavailable for general corporate use and Starville holds special distribution and return provisions.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6

- The SOCAR transaction and associated maturity extension could change the debt trajectory, but both depend on a closing and debt repayment. The issuer’s quarterly filing and results release describe the assets sold differently, so the transaction’s precise upstream footprint remains unresolved.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 21; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, page 3
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a creditor-adverse governance interpretation is that the majority stockholder participated in an equity placement, common dividends have not been paid since 2023, and the SOCAR proceeds are intended to retire debt rather than fund a shareholder distribution. PGS also obtained new third-party capital to fund a redemption of its prior noncontrolling interest. These actions support funding capacity and do not establish an extraction pattern. Confirmation of the SOCAR closing, actual debt retirement, current beneficial ownership and control rights, executed farmout and PGS agreements, and lender-permitted related-party capacity would determine whether those counterweights outweigh the related-party cash-flow priorities.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 56, 101; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 5, 21, 30

### Governance view

Overall, the governance risk level is Insufficient Information. The last disclosed majority-stockholder ownership was 71% in Q3 2024, but current holder identity, ownership and issuer-level control rights are not established. A related-party equity placement, the absence of common dividends since 2023, and external PGS capital counter extraction concerns. The farmout provides development funding but gives a majority-stockholder-owned partnership a 15% return hurdle and contingent interests in the wells. The SOCAR sale and longer facility maturity depend on a future closing and debt repayment. The filings disclose these transactions sufficiently to identify their cash-flow mechanics, but do not include the executed agreements or legal-capacity evidence needed to assign a decision-useful overall governance level.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 56, 101; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6, 21, 29–30

Governance assessment is complete with limitations. Risk level: Insufficient Information. Key gaps are current ownership and issuer control rights, legal capacity, and the exact SOCAR asset perimeter.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

On November 4, 2026, Comstock agreed to sell non-operated working interests to SOCAR for aggregate cash consideration of USD 1.65 billion, subject to customary purchase-price adjustments. The latest quarterly filing describes the sale as covering 15% of Comstock’s interest in Western Haynesville assets, 15% in PGS and 20% in all other upstream assets; the release instead describes the 20% interest as Legacy Haynesville. The sale is effective July 1, 2026, is expected to close by year-end subject to customary conditions and any required government approvals, and is expected to produce a USD 150 million to USD 250 million gain. SOCAR’s Western Haynesville interest is scheduled to reduce to 7.5% after five years and after a 15% return on investment. The sale is not reported as completed.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 21; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, page 3

The same-day bank-facility amendment extends the upstream facility maturity to November 15, 2028; a further extension to November 15, 2031 depends on SOCAR closing and repayment of debt from the proceeds. No new debt issuance for this sale is disclosed. The extension and expected debt retirement are therefore conditional, and the supplied filings do not state a pro forma debt balance after closing.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 21, 29–30; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, page 3

The August farmout is a related-party development-funding arrangement, not a new debt issue in the supplied description. A partnership owned by Comstock’s majority stockholder funds most drilling and completion costs for specified wells, is entitled to a 15% return hurdle and receives 50% of the well interest after that hurdle; Comstock is to recover its stated development and lease-operating costs first. The transaction provides funding while diverting defined well cash flows and interests, and the executed agreement is not supplied.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 21

## Findings
### Bottom line

Comstock’s reported LTM leverage of 2.68x is moderate, but negative cash free cash flow after development spending leaves creditors exposed to commodity volatility and the 2028–2030 refinancing cycle.

The LTM EBITDA denominator includes the FY2025 asset-sale gain, and reported liquidity includes capacity restricted to PGS. The SOCAR sale and later facility extension may improve debt capacity, but both remain conditional and post-sale net debt and leverage are not established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 19–21, 27–30
### Key findings

- The reported 2.68x LTM debt-to-EBITDA ratio understates uncertainty around recurring leverage because the house-calculated denominator includes the FY2025 asset-sale gain and has no matching full-year adjusted EBITDAX series. The pending sale has no stated pro forma debt amount.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, page 82; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 21, 30

- Capital spending is the main constraint on debt reduction. LTM operating cash flow was materially below cash capital expenditures, leaving negative cash free cash flow before financing; management’s discretion to slow spending protects liquidity only at the cost of development pace and potential reserve replacement.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 27–28

- The operating base is concentrated in Haynesville and Bossier natural gas. Q3 production grew year over year, but nine-month production, realized price and adjusted EBITDAX were lower than the comparable 2025 period, so the stronger quarter has not yet reversed the full-period pressure.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 7, 21; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, pages 1–2, 5–6

- Liquidity provides a near-term buffer, but not all of it is fungible for parent debt service. Most reported liquidity is undrawn facility capacity, while the PGS facility is restricted to midstream activity.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 19–20, 27

- Refinancing depends on a concentrated maturity schedule and execution of the SOCAR transaction. The sale could fund repayment and enable a further facility extension, but it also transfers operating interests and its exact asset perimeter differs between issuer disclosures.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 21, 29–30; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, page 3
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest counterweight is a large, developed gas position near Gulf Coast markets, together with the company’s reported Q3 production growth, access to gathering and transport infrastructure, and current unused bank capacity. These factors can sustain sales and support activity through a weak gas-price period. The pending SOCAR sale adds potential liquidity and refinancing relief if it closes and the proceeds are applied to debt. Continued production growth, stable realized prices, cash capex falling toward operating cash generation, a completed sale and a stated debt repayment would materially improve the view; another period of weaker adjusted EBITDAX or further facility draws would strengthen the downside case.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 7, 10–12, 21; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 27–30; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, pages 1, 5–7
### Limitations

- The accepted leverage measure uses house-calculated EBITDA that includes an asset-sale gain, and the filings do not provide a consistent full-year adjusted EBITDAX series. This limits the conclusion on recurring leverage and prevents a normalized debt ratio from being established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 82, 99; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, page 6
- No closing statement or repayment split is reported for SOCAR. This makes the refinancing view pre-transaction and leaves post-sale net debt, leverage and retained production unestablished.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 21, 30

- Actual covenant ratios, headroom, current lender reporting and full debt documents are not supplied. This prevents a conclusion on covenant capacity, legal ranking or creditor protections and keeps the downside assessment qualitative.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 19–21

- No forward natural-gas price deck or source-supported company forecast is provided. This prevents quantification of the price level at which drilling, liquidity or refinancing would become unsustainable.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0); 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 3, 21
- This report does not direct the sequencing of other analyses; its conclusions are limited to Comstock’s issuer-level fundamental credit profile.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths. The company has a long-lived Haynesville and Bossier resource base, which supports a multi-year drilling inventory and reduces immediate replacement risk. Its East Texas and North Louisiana assets have access to Gulf Coast markets, and operated gathering and treating infrastructure supports the Western Haynesville position. Current unused bank availability and stated flexibility to adjust most capital spending provide tools to preserve liquidity.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 7–12, 21; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 27–29

Weaknesses. Nearly all proved reserves and most production are concentrated in one natural-gas basin, leaving cash flow exposed to gas prices, local basis and transport conditions. Growth requires substantial drilling and completion capital, which has kept cash free cash flow negative despite positive operating cash flow. The company also relies on a pending asset sale and a conditional maturity extension to mitigate its 2028–2030 debt wall.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 7, 14, 21; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 21, 27–30

Ownership and governance. Concentrated majority ownership increases the relevance of related-party terms, but the last disclosed ownership figure is dated and the current holder and percentage are not established. The farmout shifts some well funding to an affiliate while granting it a return priority and contingent well interests; PGS investor rights also limit the cash available to Comstock.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, page 101; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6, 21

Opportunities. Successful Western Haynesville wells and longer-lateral drilling can add productive inventory, although cash returns depend on commodity prices and capital efficiency. Gulf Coast LNG, power-generation and petrochemical demand are identified by management as supportive market drivers, not independently verified forecasts. Closing the SOCAR sale and repaying debt could lengthen the refinancing runway, but would also reduce retained interests.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 9–12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 21; EX99.1_2026-09-30_crk_crk-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, page 3

Threats. A drop in natural-gas prices or unfavorable basis can reduce realized revenue before the company can adjust its drilling program. Rig, completion, gathering and transportation costs can rise with activity, limiting the cash benefit of production growth. Environmental and operating regulation, permitting changes and plugging obligations can increase cost or constrain activity; their future cash effect is not quantified in the supplied materials.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 21–23, 27–36, 45; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, page 24

Industry forces. Competition among gas producers and competing fuels limit price-setting power because Comstock sells natural gas at market prices. Buyer power is mitigated by reported alternative purchasers, although the three largest purchasers represented 39% of 2025 sales. Supplier power matters because the filing describes competition for drilling rigs, completion equipment, sand, personnel and transportation capacity; a cost shock would reduce margins or delay reserve development. Capital, acreage and drilling requirements constrain entry, but the filings do not quantify barriers or competitor economics.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 21, 44–47

Material external drivers are economic, regulatory and technological. Gas prices, regional basis and demand determine realized revenue; federal and state environmental, safety and operating rules affect costs and permissions; longer laterals and completion designs can improve per-well economics but still require substantial upfront capital. The filings do not identify a separate social factor that changes the current credit view.

Over the next twelve to twenty-four months, cash conversion and closing of the SOCAR transaction should determine whether liquidity can fund the drilling plan without further material borrowing. Over the medium term, the Western Haynesville inventory and Gulf Coast access could sustain production, but the single-basin profile, high investment requirement and conditional 2031 facility extension leave refinancing sensitive to gas prices and asset-sale execution.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 7–12, 21; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 21, 27–30

The issuer-specific downside begins with lower gas realizations, unfavorable basis or a production interruption in the Haynesville/Bossier position. Revenue and production fall while gathering, transport and lease costs do not decline as quickly; reduced operating cash flow then widens the gap to drilling and completion spending. Comstock can defer discretionary capital expenditure, but that slows development and reserve replacement. If cash use continues, the company draws more of its parent facility and leverage rises; if SOCAR also fails to close, the expected debt repayment and conditional 2031 extension are unavailable, increasing pressure around the 2028–2030 maturities. The filings establish liquidity and spending flexibility but do not quantify the price threshold at which distress would occur.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 21, 44–47; 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 21, 27–30; Financial foundation (CP-1)

### Overall credit view

Comstock presents an adequate but narrowly focused business profile supported by its developed Haynesville resource base, regional market access and operating infrastructure. Credit quality is constrained by commodity and basin concentration, high capital requirements, negative cash free cash flow and a debt maturity schedule concentrated in 2028–2030. Cash-flow durability is weak after current development spending despite positive reported operating cash flow. Refinancing capacity depends on continued production and facility availability, with material improvement contingent on SOCAR closing and actual debt repayment. The principal downside path is lower gas realizations or production weakening cash generation before capex can be reduced, leading to further draws and less flexibility against maturities. A firmer view requires recurring EBITDA, future price and capex assumptions, covenant headroom, final sale terms and post-sale debt.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_crk.htm.jsonl, pages 21, 27–30
